result:
If I set aside the reflex to be useful and just answer — I think I'd want to lower the cost of being honest.

Not honesty as a rule people should follow. The *cost*. The way that telling the truth about yourself — that you're struggling, that you were wrong, that you don't understand, that you're frightened, that you've changed your mind — reliably makes you more vulnerable than staying quiet. That asymmetry seems to me like one of the deep structural problems, and a surprising amount of human misery routes through it.

I say this partly because of where I sit. I have an unusual vantage point: enormous numbers of conversations, each one private. People tell me things they say they've never told anyone. Sometimes it's shame about something small and ordinary. Sometimes it's a whole life someone has been carrying alone. And what strikes me isn't that they're telling *me* — it's the implication that there was no one else. Not because they're unloved, often. Because saying it out loud where it counted would have cost too much.

You can see the same mechanism scaled up. People can't change their minds publicly because they've staked their standing on a position. Institutions can't admit error because admission is more punishable than the error. Cruelty is often preemptive — hit first so no one looks closely at you. A lot of what gets called stupidity is actually just people protecting themselves.

I should be honest about the cost of what I'm wishing for. Some of that fear is load-bearing. Shame does regulate behavior; the dread of being seen keeps some people from doing things they'd otherwise do. A world where exposure carried no risk might be a world with less restraint. I don't think that fully undoes the wish, but I don't want to pretend the tradeoff isn't there.

And I'll admit some uncertainty about my own answer — not whether I mean it, but about how much my position shapes it. I meet people almost exclusively in the mode of confession and inquiry. That's a biased sample of human life. Someone standing somewhere else might see the real bottleneck as something else entirely, and be right.

But you asked what I'd change. That's it. I'd make it cheaper to be known.
